name: Nanda Devi Mela, Almora
when: Late August–September, around Nanda Ashtami in the month of Bhadrapada (lunar)
summary: Kumaon's biggest autumn festival honours the goddesses Nanda and Sunanda. In Almora, images are shaped from banana-tree trunks, worshipped at the Nanda Devi temple and carried in procession through Lal Bazaar before they are taken to the water. Nainital and other towns hold their own versions.
body: Nanda Devi is the patron goddess of Kumaon and Garhwal, linked to the mountain that carries her name. In Almora her worship is centred on the Nanda Devi temple in the old town, a Chand royal temple founded in 1688. The mela grew under the Chand kings and continues as the town's main festival, falling around Nanda Ashtami in the lunar month of Bhadrapada, usually late August or September.

The festival runs over several days. Banana trunks, chosen and brought in with ceremony, are used to shape the images of the sister goddesses Nanda and Sunanda, which are dressed, decorated and installed for worship. Folk singers, drummers and dancers perform, stalls fill the bazaar, and families from surrounding villages come into town. On the final day the images are carried in procession through Lal Bazaar and taken to be submerged in water.

Nainital holds a large Nanda Devi Mahotsav at the Naina Devi temple at the same time, and smaller fairs take place in Bageshwar and other towns. For visitors, Almora's mela is the best chance to see Kumaoni folk performance, dress and food in one place. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.
tips: Book a room at Kasar Devi or in Almora early; families return home for the mela and rooms fill.
Watch the final procession from a step or shop front in Lal Bazaar and keep children close in the crowd.
Ask before photographing rituals and performers, and do not use flash near the images.

faqs.q: When is the Nanda Devi Mela in Almora?
faqs.a: It falls around Nanda Ashtami in the lunar month of Bhadrapada, usually in late August or September. Exact dates change each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What happens at the Nanda Devi Mela?
faqs.a: Images of the goddesses Nanda and Sunanda are shaped from banana trunks and worshipped at the Nanda Devi temple, with folk music, dance and stalls in the bazaar, ending in a procession to the water.

faqs.q: Is the Nanda Devi Mela held in Nainital too?
faqs.a: Yes, Nainital holds a large Nanda Devi Mahotsav at the Naina Devi temple at the same time of year, with its own procession. Bageshwar and other towns hold smaller fairs.

faqs.q: Is the Nanda Devi Mela suitable for tourists?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors are welcome. It is crowded on the main days, so be patient, dress modestly, respect rituals and keep valuables secure. Late monsoon rain is possible.

name: Jageshwar Shravan festival
when: July–August, the Hindu month of Shravan (lunar), busiest on Mondays
summary: During Shravan, the monsoon month sacred to Shiva, Jageshwar's ancient temple valley fills with pilgrims, puja and fairs. The Jageshwar Monsoon Festival runs through the month, with crowds peaking on Mondays and bells and chants echoing among the deodars.
body: Shravan, which overlaps July and August, is the holiest month of the year for Shiva's devotees, and Jageshwar is one of the most important Shiva sites in Kumaon. Through the month the valley hosts what is called the Jageshwar Monsoon Festival, with daily puja, special rituals, and a fair along the road between the Dandeshwar and Jageshwar temples.

Pilgrims come from across Kumaon and beyond, many on Mondays, the day most associated with Shiva. They bathe, offer water and bel leaves to the lingams and arrange rituals with temple priests; making and worshipping clay lingams is a common Shravan practice here. Stalls sell offerings, sweets and household goods, and folk music adds to the atmosphere in the evenings.

It is also the height of the monsoon. Roads from Almora can be blocked by landslides, the stone courtyards are wet, and mist hangs in the deodar trees. For travellers, a weekday visit in Shravan gives the feel of the festival with smaller crowds. Keep spare days, travel in daylight and check current status before you travel.
tips: Visit on a weekday rather than a Monday if you want to move around the temples comfortably.
Carry rain gear and shoes with grip; courtyards and paths are slippery.
Stay overnight in Jageshwar or Almora rather than driving back in the dark on monsoon roads.

faqs.q: When is the Jageshwar Monsoon Festival?
faqs.a: It runs through the Hindu month of Shravan, which falls in July and August depending on the lunar calendar. Mondays are the busiest days. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it safe to travel to Jageshwar in Shravan?
faqs.a: It is the monsoon, so landslides and road closures are possible. Travel in daylight, allow buffer days, follow local advice and check road status each morning.

faqs.q: What rituals take place at Jageshwar in Shravan?
faqs.a: Pilgrims offer water, milk and bel leaves to the lingams, arrange puja with priests, and many take part in worship of clay lingams. A fair runs along the valley road.

faqs.q: Can non-Hindus visit during the Shravan festival?
faqs.a: Visitors are generally welcome in the temple courtyards. Dress modestly, remove shoes, avoid photographing rituals without permission and follow any restrictions at the sanctum.

name: Harela
when: Mid-July, first day of Shravan (Kark Sankranti, solar calendar)
summary: Harela, the day of green, marks the start of the monsoon and the sowing season in Kumaon. Families sow five or seven kinds of seed ten days earlier, then cut the young shoots on the day and place them on their heads as a blessing. Today it is also a tree-planting day.
body: Harela is celebrated across Uttarakhand but has its strongest roots in Kumaon. It falls on the first day of the month of Shravan in the solar calendar, Kark Sankranti, usually around 16 or 17 July. The name means the day of green, and the festival welcomes the monsoon and the start of the sowing cycle for farming families.

About ten days before the festival, the head of each household sows five or seven kinds of seed, such as wheat, barley, maize and pulses, in small baskets or pots of soil and waters them daily. On Harela the yellow-green seedlings, also called harela, are cut, offered to the household deities, and placed on the heads and behind the ears of family members with blessings. Children sometimes play gedi, walking on bamboo stilts.

In recent years Harela has become closely tied to the environment, and schools, villages and government offices plant saplings on the day. Kumaon also observes smaller Harela-linked rituals during the Chaitra and Ashwin Navratris. For visitors, the festival is a home ritual rather than a public show, so the best way to see it is through a homestay.
tips: Stay in a village homestay in mid-July if you want to see the household ritual.
Join a local tree-planting event if one is organised where you stay.
Remember it is monsoon: plan short, flexible drives around the date.

faqs.a: Harela falls on Kark Sankranti, the first day of Shravan in the solar calendar, usually around 16 or 17 July. Seeds are sown about ten days earlier.

faqs.q: What is the meaning of Harela?
faqs.a: Harela means the day of green. It celebrates the monsoon and the start of sowing, with prayers for a good harvest and prosperity.

faqs.q: How is Harela celebrated in Kumaon?
faqs.a: Families sow five or seven kinds of seed ten days before. On the day the seedlings are cut, offered to the deities and placed on family members' heads with blessings. Tree planting has become part of the day.

faqs.q: Can tourists take part in Harela?
faqs.a: Harela is mostly a household festival, so tourists see it best by staying with a family in a village homestay. Many towns also hold public tree-planting events that visitors can join.
